name: Colorpuncture

lead: Colorpuncture applies coloured light, rather than needles, to acupuncture points on the body. The best-known form, Esogetic Colorpuncture Therapy, was developed by Peter Mandel and is delivered by trained complementary-medicine practitioners.

Practitioners describe it as a non-invasive, holistic method aimed at overall wellbeing, and its connection to looks is via that wider framing (feeling and appearing more rested and balanced) rather than a targeted cosmetic effect. Published human reports consist of small European pilot studies and individual case reports.

paras: A session typically involves a practitioner placing a light probe fitted with a coloured filter or crystal on chosen points or zones for a short time each, usually as part of a course of visits. It is often combined with other holistic therapies. Timelines and protocols are set by individual practitioners.

Because no needles are inserted, the technique is generally described as non-invasive. Researchers note that the available studies are small pilot or case-report designs, so effects on specific conditions have not been established in controlled trials. Anyone using it for a medical condition may want to continue conventional care alongside it, as health agencies generally advise for complementary therapies.

angle.text: Practitioners present colorpuncture as a gentle whole-body treatment, so any look benefit is the claimed knock-on of feeling better and more balanced. It is not marketed in these sources as a targeted skin or facial treatment.

lead: Colorpuncture is a form of acu-light therapy in which coloured light is applied to acupuncture points or meridian zones instead of needles. Its best-known system, Esogetic Colorpuncture Therapy (ECT), was devised by Peter Mandel and is described by its proponents as a holistic method for body, mind and spirit. [1][2]

People come to it mainly for general wellbeing; its link to appearance is the one practitioners draw between inner balance, rest and vitality and how a person looks and feels. The documented applications are health-related (for example migraine, sleep and respiratory complaints) rather than cosmetic procedures. [1]

Published literature on colorpuncture is small. A 1999 review of European studies on ECT described them as pilot or preliminary research because of limited design and sample size, while reporting symptom improvement in each. [1] Other items are case reports, a laboratory study on chick brain cells and a single-patient photon-emission study. [3][4][5]

paras: Colorpuncture belongs to the family of light-based acupuncture techniques. Rather than puncturing the skin, the practitioner directs light of a chosen colour onto points associated with traditional Chinese medicine meridians, with colours matched to organs and functions according to the system's theory. [3][2]

A 1999 overview traced colour therapy from ancient Egypt to modern light therapy for seasonal affective disorder, and discussed Mandel's Colorpuncture and McWilliams's Chromo-pressure as contemporary systems. [3] The author of that overview raised the hypothesis, drawing on Russian research, that acupuncture meridians might conduct light in the body somewhat like optical fibre. [3]
Proponents of Esogetic Colorpuncture describe it as an acu-light system for treating the whole person, and report fast, economical and non-toxic results for selected complaints. [1][2]

The theoretical framework draws on traditional Oriental medicine, relating colours to internal organs and meridians. [3] Acupuncture itself is, according to Wikipedia's summary of systematic reviews, an area where many reviewers find little robust evidence beyond a few conditions; colorpuncture has not been separately assessed in such reviews. [6]

A 1999 review in the American Journal of Acupuncture summarised European studies of ECT in migraine, childhood insomnia, bronchitis, attention and learning disorders, and uterine fibroids. Its author stressed that design and sample-size limitations mean these should be seen as pilot research, while reporting marked symptom improvement in all of them. [1]

A 2002 letter described treatment of post-herpetic neuralgia with colorpuncture, and a 2008 case report followed spontaneous photon emission in one person with multiple sclerosis across 22 sessions, reporting changes in a derived coherency index and relief of symptoms. [4][5] A laboratory study found that red-light colorpuncture sped recovery of calcium levels in clinorotated chick-embryo brain cells. [7] No controlled trial of colorpuncture for skin or other cosmetic outcomes has been published.
No adverse-event series specific to colorpuncture has been published. Acupuncture proper carries reported infection and injury risks tied to needles, which colorpuncture does not use. [6]
